claims.quote: To be clear GenCost agrees that high capacity factors of around 90% are achievable for nuclear generation. The observed global average capacity factor for nuclear generation is 80% and 10% of nuclear generation is operating at below 60%.

claims.quote: GenCost bases its capacity factor assumptions for all baseload technologies – coal, gas, and nuclear – on the Australian evidence, applying a maximum of 89% and minimum of 53%. The minimum is based on the same formula that we apply to renewables (the minimum capacity factor for new build generation is assumed to be 10% below the average capacity factor of existing equivalent generation).
claims.locator: GenCost 2024-25 Final report, Section 2.2 (verified against official accessible-text file)
claims.whatItClaims: The 53-89% range is derived from Australian coal-fleet experience via a formula applied consistently across technologies — the report's consistency defence against cherry-picking accusations.

assumptions.assumption: A technology-by-technology unit-cost comparison (LCOE plus itemised integration costs) is an adequate frame for ranking generation options for a whole electricity system.
assumptions.evidence: GenCost 2024-25 Final, Executive summary: integration costs 'include storage, transmission, system security and spilled energy'; FAQ: 'LCOE is only meaningful as a quick guide to competitiveness.'
assumptions.contested: Frontier Economics built its whole case on rejecting this frame in favour of total system cost; CSIRO effectively conceded the point in 2025-26 by introducing SLCOE ('LCOE does not include renewable integration costs. SLCOE does.') — an audit should note the measure changed after the fight, not before it.

assumptions.assumption: Australian coal-fleet operating history (average 59%, max 89%) is the right reference class for predicting Australian nuclear capacity factors.
assumptions.evidence: GenCost 2024-25 Final Section 2.2: baseload capacity factors for 'coal, gas, and nuclear' are based 'on the Australian evidence, applying a maximum of 89% and minimum of 53%'; the nuclear explainer makes the steam-turbine analogy explicit.
assumptions.contested: Nuclear advocates say the relevant class is the operating global/US nuclear fleet (US average 93%, global average 80%); CIS (Hilton) argues internal inconsistency — GenCost's own merit-order logic for cheap-fuel brown coal (90%) should apply to cheap-fuel nuclear. CSIRO's rebuttal: 'a prudent investor... must prepare for all plausible eventualities.'

assumptions.assumption: A 30-year capital-recovery period (financing convention) rather than engineering life is what determines the cost consumers pay.
assumptions.evidence: FAQ: 'It's standard practice that the financing period for an asset is less than its full operational life, similar to a car or house loan.'
assumptions.contested: Frontier amortises over 50 years and calls even that unrealistically short; critics say 30 years roughly doubles nuclear's apparent capital charge. CSIRO's 60-year sensitivity found only an 8% average cost reduction after 'substantial reinvestment' — but that 8% figure depends on assumed refurbishment costs and on renewables' assumed cost declines when 'built twice', both auditable.

assumptions.assumption: A first-of-a-kind premium of up to 120% (from Flyvbjerg & Gardner's general megaproject cost-overrun research) transfers to Australian nuclear.
assumptions.evidence: GenCost 2024-25 Final Section 3.1.1: 'the value of 120% has been applied to large scale nuclear based on Flyvbjerg and Gardner (2023)'; carried into 2025-26 (draft Table 2-1: 120%/60% large nuclear, 92%/46% SMR).
assumptions.contested: Advocates argue an experienced foreign vendor (Korea, UAE model) would not pay a full FOAK premium; conversely the premium is applied to a South-Korea-derived base cost that critics like IEEFA/CEC say is already below recent Western experience ($15,000-$28,000/kW) — the premium can be attacked as both too high and too low depending on the base.

assumptions.assumption: Total development time (site, permits, financing, grid studies) — not just construction — is the relevant timeline, giving 'at least 15 years' for first Australian nuclear power.
assumptions.evidence: GenCost 2024-25 Final Section 2.3; FAQ lists pre-construction activities; explainer: 'at least 15 years after legal restrictions were removed'.
assumptions.contested: Critics cite IAEA's 10-15 years and the UAE's fast build; CSIRO counters that recent median construction alone is 8.2 years and that no-industry, first-mover democracies are slower. The clock also assumes repeal of the ban, which as of Feb 2026 had not occurred.

assumptions.assumption: Costs of the existing pre-2030 system (and policy-driven renewables build already underway) can be treated as given/sunk when comparing new-build options.
assumptions.evidence: GenCost 2024-25: 'All new capacity relies on being supported by existing generation capacity to meet demand'; GenCost 2025-26 exec summary concedes for 2030 SLCOE that 'there is no consistent rule or readily available data for capturing the amount of unrecovered costs associated with that capacity' and swaps in futures prices instead.
assumptions.contested: The long-running critic claim (CIS/Aidan Morrison lineage) is that this hides the renewables transition's cumulative system costs; CSIRO's 2025-26 retreat on 2030 SLCOE is the closest it has come to acknowledging the measurement gap.

assumptions.assumption: Costs excluded from GenCost (nuclear waste storage, insurance, decommissioning detail) 'won't significantly affect a technology's competitive position'.
assumptions.evidence: FAQ waste-storage answer (quoted verbatim in claims).
assumptions.contested: CEC turns the same materiality question on Frontier ('unclear whether and how Frontier has accounted for nuclear waste management and insurance costs'); the materiality judgment is asserted, not demonstrated, in the public-facing material.

assumptions.assumption: Frontier's headline requires that AEMO's Progressive (lower-demand) scenario is the appropriate base case for Coalition policy, that nuclear costs $10,000/kW with 1%/yr learning, that plants amortise over 50 years at ~90% utilisation, and that 65% of the coal fleet can run past announced closure dates within existing O&M budgets.
assumptions.evidence: Frontier Report 2, Sections 1.3-1.5 and 3.2.3 (all quoted verbatim in claims); the 44% figure compares Progressive-with-nuclear against Step-Change-without, while the like-for-like figure is 25%.
assumptions.contested: CEC/IEEFA: capex understated vs $15,000-$28,000/kW international experience, O&M+fuel understated vs GenCost's $40-$60/MWh, coal-extension costs unevidenced ('little evidence provided within the report to evaluate the realism of this claim'); CSIRO: the scenario design means the report 'cannot be used to draw any conclusions about the cost of nuclear generation relative to other generation options'; academics note Frontier publishes no LCOE or capacity factor, making the numbers hard to probe.

assumptions.assumption: Electricity futures prices are a valid substitute indicator for 2030 generation costs (GenCost 2025-26's replacement for 2030 SLCOE).
assumptions.evidence: GenCost 2025-26 exec summary: futures 'rely on market expectations rather than modelling'; $80-$90/MWh by 2030 cited in the final news release.
assumptions.contested: Futures embed policy expectations and existing-fleet dynamics, so they answer a different question than 'what does the new-build mix cost' — a quiet change of measure between editions that an audit should surface.

assumptions.assumption: The political argument built on GenCost assumed its rankings translate into deliverable policy; the counter-argument built on Frontier assumed its system savings survive contact with financing and construction reality.
assumptions.evidence: Election outcome: Coalition lost May 2025; post-election the policy shrank to 'lift the ban on nuclear power' (Tehan's principles, Nov 2025) and the ban remained law at the 4 Feb 2026 Senate second-reading debate.
assumptions.contested: Both sides treat the other's report as politically motivated: Frontier consulted the Coalition while claiming sole direction; GenCost is commissioned by AEMO, whose ISP the Coalition's plan would overturn — each provenance claim is itself audit material.

gencost.context: EDITION MAP (corrects the task brief): the nuclear fight ran on the GenCost 2024-25 DRAFT (released 9 Dec 2024) and the 2024-25 FINAL — which CSIRO's news page dates 29 July 2025, not June 2025 as the brief assumed. The latest edition as of today is GenCost 2025-26 FINAL, released 15 July 2026 (draft 17 Dec 2025). The 2025-26 edition changed the argument's structure: it introduced SLCOE (whole-system levelised cost, including transmission) alongside LCOE, published an open-source Simple Electricity Model, and — after stakeholder pushback — replaced its 2030 SLCOE estimate with electricity futures prices because there is 'no consistent rule' for counting unrecovered costs of existing capacity. That concession is the closest CSIRO has come to validating the critics' 'hidden system costs' line, and any audit should treat the LCOE→SLCOE evolution as CSIRO amending its own measure under criticism. POLITICAL ARC: Frontier Economics' two reports (14 Nov and 13 Dec 2024) — 'funded and directed solely by Frontier' but produced in consultation with the Federal Coalition — supplied the Coalition's $331b/44%-cheaper nuclear costings; Labor won the 3 May 2025 election; under Sussan Ley the seven-reactor plan went into limbo (May 2025) and by 13 Nov 2025 the Liberals had dropped net zero, with nuclear policy reduced to 'lift the ban on nuclear power' among Dan Tehan's ten principles. assumptions.assumption: The Progressive Change demand profile is the correct basis for costing the nuclear pathway, while Step Change is the correct basis for the ISP pathway — i.e. the comparison may legitimately cross demand scenarios.
assumptions.evidence: Report 2 s1.3.4: the Federal Coalition 'confirmed that they consider the demand forecast embodied in the Progressive scenario is more consistent with their view'; Frontier adds AEMO rates Progressive 42% likely vs 43% for Step Change. assumptions.contested: The single most contested move. Baldwin (Scimex): 'comparing apples with oranges as they yield two different emissions outcomes'. Bowyer (IEEFA): 'these are not like-for-like'. CEC: Progressive represents '26 per cent lower electricity demand'; 'Lower demand requires a smaller system build, and a lower capital spend.' Within-scenario, Frontier's own numbers show only 25% savings — the 44% headline needs the scenario crossing.

assumptions.assumption: Total system cost (sum of undiscounted real costs, 2025–2051) is the right decision metric; LCOE and NPV presentations are inferior or misleading.
assumptions.evidence: Report 2 s1.1 calls generator-level comparison 'incorrect and misleading'; AEC records Frontier's argument that 'consumers don't pay the NPV, they pay the real costs'. NPV tables are included (7% real WACC, stated only in Report 1) but relegated; Report 2's WACC footnote is a broken cross-reference.
assumptions.contested: AEC (sympathetic-neutral): 'it would be useful to have both quoted' and the report 'could have been enhanced' by an LCOE. Undiscounted sums over 26 years inflate all totals and favour the pathway that defers capex (nuclear starts 2036); CEC notes Frontier's NPV of the ISP ($225bn) is nearly double AEMO's own $122bn because it adds O&M/fuel/emissions to a capital-only figure.

assumptions.evidence: Report 2 s1.4 bullets; robustness claim that assumed costs 'could double on a sustained basis' before parity is lost; Price's AFR op-ed cites unnamed 'excellent recent examples of projects that are far less costly'.

frontier.context: STRUCTURE OF THE ARGUMENT (for auditing Frontier as an argument, not summarising it). The two reports form a two-step syllogism. Report 1 ('Report 1 – Developing a base case to assess the relative costs of nuclear power in the NEM', dated 14 November 2024) argues (a) the right cost metric is whole-of-system real cost, not LCOE; (b) Frontier's model replicates AEMO's 2024 ISP closely (AEC: '97 per cent aligned' on NPV), so it can be trusted to run counterfactuals AEMO refuses to run; (c) properly counted, the Step Change ISP pathway costs $580bn + $62bn transmission = $642bn. Report 2 ('Report 2 - Economic analysis of including nuclear power in the NEM', released 13 December 2024 — the landing page and CEC both date it 13 Dec; the PDF itself carries no date on the extracted pages) then swaps nuclear into both AEMO scenarios and reports four cells of a 2x2 (scenario x nuclear): $594/$446/$437/$331bn. The headline '44% cheaper' is the diagonal of that 2x2 — it changes demand scenario AND technology simultaneously. Frontier states this openly (s1.5.1) and justifies the diagonal via s1.3.4: the Coalition 'confirmed' Progressive matches their worldview, plus AEMO's own 42%-vs-43% scenario likelihoods. Every serious critic attacks the diagonal (Baldwin 'apples with oranges', Bowyer 'not like-for-like', CEC '26 per cent lower electricity demand'); Frontier's defenders reply that costing a party's policy on that party's demand outlook is legitimate scenario analysis. That is the crux for the structural audit: is the warrant 'a party may choose its own demand scenario' strong enough to carry a comparative-cost headline used against the other party's scenario? Secondary contested moves, each with claim+counterclaim in the bank: undiscounted sum-of-real-costs headlining (with NPV at 7% real WACC relegated, and Report 2's WACC footnote literally broken: 'Error! Reference source not found.'); the $10,000/kW + $30/MWh + 1% learning nuclear inputs vs observed builds; 2036 first power vs GenCost's ≥15-year lead time; 65% coal-fleet life-extension with no refurbishment/subsidy/outage costs; the 2051 truncation vs 50-year amortisation tail (Price's annualisation defence vs IEEFA/CEC); emissions treated as overstated-by-baseline rather than costed (VER excluded); and symmetric exclusions (CER/DSP/distribution/REZ) inherited from the ISP's own scope. Note Frontier's asymmetric aside that AEMO's path will really cost 'well above a trillion dollars' — un-modelled editorialising inside a modelling report. DEFENCES: the primary defence document is Danny Price's AFR op-ed (published 18 Dec 2024, free full text on Frontier's site, 20 Dec post) responding to Steven Hamilton's AFR critique of 16 Dec 2024 (paywalled; Hamilton's points are reconstructable only via Price's characterisation — flag this if quoting). Price also blasted critics as having 'a vested interest' in Capital Brief (Jan 2025, paywalled preview — not fetched, do not quote). TIMELINE/CURRENCY (all verified this session, 21 July 2026): Labor won the 3 May 2025 election in a landslide and Dutton lost his seat; Ley replaced him; the Nationals briefly split from the Liberals in May 2025 with nuclear/energy disagreement cited; per AAP (9 Nov 2025) the reunion deal made 'lifting the ban' the coalition-agreement nuclear commitment, Tehan flagged possible coal subsidies, and the Coalition then dumped its net-zero-by-2050 commitment (The Conversation, 18 Nov 2025). The seven-reactor, Commonwealth-owned, Frontier-costed build program is no longer operative policy — the live Coalition position is ban-repeal. The federal ban (EPBC Act s140A + ARPANS Act) remains IN FORCE: on 4 Feb 2026 Canavan moved the second reading of the private senators' Removing Nuclear Energy Prohibitions Bill 2026 and debate was adjourned; treat any claim that 'Australia lifted the ban in 2026' as false (it circulates on SEO sites). The evidential base has also moved: GenCost 2025-26 final is released (solar+wind still least-cost; nuclear cost trends INCREASING), and AEMO's 2026 ISP (25 June 2026) supersedes the 2024 ISP Frontier modelled. No 2025/2026 update to either Frontier report was found. GenCost draft itself: "In any given year, we are readily able to change assumptions..."

Frontier/O'Brien say Progressive Change matches actual Coalition policy (slower renewables build-out); critics say costing two different demand futures against each other is the central trick producing the 44% figure.

assumptions.assumption: Both reports use broadly similar nuclear capital costs per kW — the headline gap comes from other parameters (capacity factor, plant life, scenario, learning rates).

assumptions.contested: Yes, from both flanks: Quiggin says the Czech Dukovany contract (~50% above GenCost's estimate) shows BOTH are too low; Price says recent projects come in "far less costly than what I have used and even lower than recommended by the CSIRO". assumptions.assumption: First Australian nuclear power arrives 2036 (Frontier/Coalition) vs ~2040s (GenCost, AEMO, House committee).

current.context: CURRENT-STATE BANK, compiled 2026-07-21, for The Whetstone nuclear-Australia briefing set (parent + two report reviews). The picture as of today, in one arc: (1) POLITICS. The 3 May 2025 election was a Labor landslide (94-43); Dutton, the seven-reactor plan's sponsor, lost his own seat. The Coalition then spent 2025 reviewing; on ~12 November 2025 Ley and Tehan announced the Liberals were dumping net zero, with the nuclear plank reduced to a principle of 'lifting the ban'. On 13 February 2026 Angus Taylor took the leadership 34-17 (Ley quit parliament; Farrer by-election). Taylor's May 2026 Budget reply set current policy: 'We will lift the ban' — no sites, no reactor count, no government-build commitment. The seven-sites plan has not been revived; write it as superseded, not formally scrapped (no formal abandonment statement found). (2) LEGAL BAN. Federal EPBC/ARPANS prohibitions still in force — proven by Canavan's repeal bill being at second reading on 4 Feb 2026 and Taylor's lift-the-ban pledge. The genuinely new fact: NSW's Legislative Council passed Ruddick's repeal bill on 7 May 2026 (introduced 11 Nov 2025, NSW Coalition backing announced 11 Feb 2026) — the first Australian chamber to vote to repeal a nuclear/uranium ban — but it has NOT passed the Labor-controlled Assembly and is not law. Qld and Vic bans untouched. (3) COSTINGS. Two new authoritative editions post-date the 2024-25 fight: GenCost 2025-26 (draft 17 Dec 2025; FINAL 15 July 2026 — check it, it is 6 days old) and AEMO's 2026 ISP (draft 10 Dec 2025; FINAL 25 June 2026). Both reaffirm renewables-least-cost; the ISP's optimal path contains no nuclear; GenCost's draft found adding nuclear raises system-level average costs and revised large-scale nuclear costs UP (South Korea benchmark via coal-cost ratio; FOAK premium still excluded from published figures). No new Frontier Economics costing located after June 2025. (4) DID THE FIGHT MOVE? Partially. CSIRO effectively conceded the critics' strongest structural point by building a system-level method (SLCOE) — Clayton Utz (11 Mar 2026) reads it as a direct response to the LCOE-understates-system-costs critique — and open-sourced its model (SEM). But the sceptic side (now led publicly by CIS/Aidan Morrison, submission 2 Feb 2026) rejects SLCOE's boundary choices (~$74bn of committed projects treated as sunk), so the dispute relocated rather than resolved. GenCost 2024-25's FINAL (29 July 2025) held the SMR-most-expensive line even with Darlington data.
